title: Literary Devices in Depth
bigQuestion: When a text can be read more than one way, how do we decide which readings are strong and which are only guesses?

story.title: The Man Who Says He Is Not Mad
story.kicker: A story from 1843 opens with a narrator arguing with you before you have said a word, and the argument is the whole point.
paragraphs: The first sentence of Edgar Allan Poe's story The Tell-Tale Heart is a defense. The narrator admits he has been nervous, dreadfully nervous, and then turns on the reader: why will you say that I am mad? Nobody has said it yet. The story is one paragraph old, and already the man telling it is answering an accusation that only he can hear. That is the first clue, and Poe hands it to you on purpose.

The narrator goes on to prove his sanity in the strangest way possible. He explains how carefully he planned to kill an old man he lived with, a man who had never wronged him. He hated the old man's pale blue eye, which he calls a vulture eye. For seven nights he eased the door open at midnight and shone a single ray of lantern light on the sleeping face. On the eighth night the eye was open. He killed the old man, cut up the body and hid the pieces under the floorboards. Then he sat the police down in chairs right over the spot, calm and smiling.

Every detail he offers to show how clever and calm he was shows the opposite. A sane man does not count his slow, silent steps toward a stranger's bed as evidence of his good judgment. The reader is doing two things at once: hearing the story the narrator tells, and building a second story, the true one, out of what he lets slip. That gap between the teller's version and the reader's version is where much of the power of literature lives.

The ending closes the gap. Sitting with the police, the narrator begins to hear a low, dull, quick sound, like a watch wrapped in cotton. He decides it is the dead man's heart beating under the boards. The officers hear nothing. The sound grows until he cannot bear it, and he tears up the floor and confesses. The heart he hears is, of course, his own. He never understands that. You do.

This chapter is about the tools writers use to make readers see more than characters see: unreliable narrators, irony, structure, symbols, allusion, satire. It is also about what to do when two careful readers see different things in the same lines. Poe's narrator wants you to accept one reading. The story quietly insists on another. Learning to weigh the two is what literary interpretation means.
story.think: The narrator gives evidence of his sanity and the reader takes it as evidence of the opposite. What kind of evidence would have actually convinced you he was sane?

lessons.title: Structure Carries Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: The order in which a text gives you its events is a choice, and the choice changes what the events mean.
reading: Read these two openings of the same story. First: Maria was born in Pilsen in 1998, went to school on Eighteenth Street, and learned to sew from her grandmother. Second: The dress was finished at three in the morning, and Maria sat on the floor beside it and cried, because her grandmother would never see it. Both openings are true to the same story. The first starts at the beginning and marches forward. The second starts at the end of something and leaves you wanting to know why.

The arrangement of a text's parts is its *structure*. A writer can tell events in the order they happened, which is *chronological* order, or begin in the middle of the action, a device with a Latin name, *in medias res*. A writer can jump backward in a *flashback*, hold back a key fact until the last page, or tell the same night from three characters' points of view. None of these choices is neutral. Starting with the finished dress makes grief the subject; starting with the birth makes a whole life the subject.

When you analyze structure, ask two questions. What do I know at each point, and what does the character know? Poe's narrator tells his story after the crime, so he knows the ending, and his attempts to prove himself calm are shadowed by what we sense is coming. A mystery hides the answer until the end so the reader hunts. A tragedy often tells you the ending in the prologue so you watch the characters walk toward it. The gap between what you know and when you learn it is a tool the writer controls.

A useful habit: after you finish a text, sketch its skeleton. Where does it start in time? Where does it jump? Where does it slow down and give a single moment three pages, and where does it cover ten years in a sentence? The places a writer spends the most words are usually the places the writer thinks matter most. Structure is an argument about importance, made without a single sentence of explanation.

words.d: the way a text's parts are arranged: the order of events, where it starts, where it slows or jumps
in the order events happened in time
a Latin phrase, 'into the middle of things': beginning a story in the middle of the action
a scene that interrupts the present action to show something from earlier

look.title: Two Skeletons
look.text: Story A: a soldier's childhood, his enlistment, the battle, his return home, his old age. Story B: an old man on a porch; the battle in one long flashback; the porch again as the sun sets. Same soldier, same battle.
look.prompt: Which story is about the battle, and which is about living with the battle afterward? How does the structure alone tell you?

check.q: A novel begins with a car crash and only later explains who was driving and why. What device is that?
choices: Chronological order
In medias res
A motif
Satire
check.why: Beginning in the middle of the action, before the causes are explained, is in medias res.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the two openings about Maria have different subjects?
choices: The second opening has a grammar error
The first opening is fiction and the second is not
Starting with the finished dress makes grief the subject; starting with her birth makes a whole life the subject
The first opening is written in the present tense
check.why: Both are true to the same story, but where a text starts decides what it is about.

check.q: According to the lesson, what does the amount of space a writer gives a moment usually show?
choices: How long the moment took in real time
That the writer ran out of other material
That the moment is unimportant
How important the writer thinks the moment is
check.why: Writers spend the most words on what they think matters most; structure argues about importance without saying so.

lessons.title: The Narrator You Cannot Trust
lessons.mainIdea: An unreliable narrator tells a story the reader must read against, using the teller's own slips as evidence.
reading: Here is a narrator: I only borrowed my sister's phone for a minute, and it is not my fault it fell in the pool, and anyway she is always leaving it around. You have not met this person, but you already suspect that the minute was longer, the fall was not an accident, and the sister is not the problem. A narrator whose version of events the reader learns to doubt is an *unreliable narrator*. The unreliability is not a mistake by the author. It is the author's design.

Narrators can be unreliable for different reasons. Some lie on purpose to look better. Some are children who do not understand what they are seeing. Some are mad, like Poe's narrator, who describes his own madness in the act of denying it. Some are simply too close to the events to judge them. In every case the author plants *evidence* that points past the narrator: a fact that does not fit, a reaction that is too strong, another character who sees things differently.

Reading an unreliable narrator well means keeping two ledgers. In one, write what the narrator claims. In the other, write what the details show. Poe's narrator claims he acted with the calm of a healthy mind. The details show a man who spent seven nights creeping into a room to stare at an eye, then heard a dead heart through a floor. When the two ledgers disagree, the second one is usually the truth of the story, and the distance between them is the story's meaning.

Be careful, though. Not every first-person narrator is unreliable, and calling every narrator a liar is a lazy reading. The test is evidence. Can you point to specific lines where the narrator's account cracks? If you can, you have an interpretation. If you cannot, you have a suspicion, and a suspicion is not yet an argument.

words.d: a storyteller whose account the reader has reason to doubt, by the author's design
narration told by a character using 'I'
specific details in the text that support a reading of it

look.title: A Defense Before the Charge
look.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses—not destroyed—not dulled them.
look.cite: Edgar Allan Poe, The Tell-Tale Heart, 1843
look.prompt: The narrator admits a disease and denies madness in the same breath. Which words in these two sentences work against his claim?

check.q: What is an unreliable narrator?
choices: A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt, by the author's design
A narrator who tells the story in the third person
A narrator the author accidentally made confusing
A narrator who never uses the word 'I'
check.why: The unreliability is a deliberate choice by the author, and the reader is meant to read against it.

check.q: What does the lesson say is the test for calling a narrator unreliable?
choices: Whether the narrator is a child
Whether you can point to specific lines where the account cracks
Whether the story is told in the past tense
Whether the narrator is the main character
check.why: A suspicion is not an argument. Evidence in the text makes the reading an interpretation.

check.q: In the two-ledger method, what usually turns out to be the truth of the story?
choices: What the narrator claims
Whatever the reader prefers
What the details show
The title of the story
check.why: When the narrator's claims and the details disagree, the details point to the story's real meaning.

lessons.title: Setting and Order as Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Where and when a writer places a story, and in what order the reader meets its parts, are decisions that shape everything the story can mean.
reading: Put the same argument between a mother and a son in three places: a kitchen at dinner, a hospital hallway at two in the morning, a parked car outside a courthouse. The words can stay exactly the same. The meaning cannot. *Setting* is the time and place of a story, and it is never just scenery. It tells the reader what is at stake, what the characters can and cannot do, and what the world around them expects.

Setting works on more than one scale. The largest scale is the historical moment: a story set in Chicago in 1919, the summer of the race riot, carries a weight that the same story set in 2019 does not. The middle scale is the social world, such as a small town where everyone knows everyone, or a city where no one does. The smallest scale is the room. Poe locks his narrator and the old man in one dark house, and the closeness makes the story feel like a trap.

Order works with setting. A writer who shows you the empty house first and the family second has decided that loss is the frame. A writer who shows the family first lets you love them before you lose them. Ask of any text: why here, why now, and why in this order? If you can imagine the same events in another place or another sequence, and you can say how the meaning would change, you have understood the author's choice instead of simply accepting it.

A short exercise makes this real. Take a scene you know, from a story or from your own life, and move it. Change the season. Change the city. Tell the ending first. Notice what breaks and what suddenly becomes visible. Writers do this all the time in revision, and readers who can do it in their heads read with the writer's eyes.

words.d: the time and place of a story, at every scale from the historical moment to the room
what a character stands to gain or lose in a situation
the opening situation through which a reader sees everything that follows

look.title: One Argument, Three Rooms
look.text: A son tells his mother he is dropping out of college. Version one: at the kitchen table on a Sunday. Version two: in the hospital hallway where his father is being treated. Version three: in the car outside the courthouse where the son has just paid a fine.
look.prompt: In which version is the mother most likely to be angry, and in which most likely to be afraid? What in each setting produces that difference?

check.q: Which scale of setting does the lesson say makes Poe's story feel like a trap?
choices: The historical moment
The social world of the town
The single dark house
The weather
check.why: The smallest scale, the room or house, closes the narrator and the old man together.

check.q: What does the lesson mean by saying setting is 'never just scenery'?
choices: Setting is always described in long paragraphs
Setting tells the reader what is at stake and what the world expects of the characters
Setting must always be a real place
Setting only matters in historical fiction
check.why: The time and place shape what characters can do and what their actions mean.

check.q: Which question does the lesson recommend asking about any text's setting and order?
choices: How many characters are there?
Is the narrator reliable?
What is the theme?
Why here, why now, and why in this order?
check.why: Imagining the events elsewhere or in another sequence shows what the author's actual choice accomplishes.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Irony
lessons.mainIdea: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or true, and it comes in verbal, situational and dramatic forms.
reading: A student walks into class soaked from the rain and says, Beautiful day. That is *verbal irony*: the words say one thing and mean the opposite, and both speaker and listener know it. Sarcasm is verbal irony with an edge meant to wound. But irony is much bigger than sarcasm, and its other forms do the heaviest work in literature.

*Situational irony* is a gap between what is expected and what happens. In O. Henry's story The Gift of the Magi, from 1905, a poor young wife sells her long hair to buy a chain for her husband's watch, while he sells the watch to buy combs for her hair. Each gift is made useless by the other. The irony is not in anyone's words; it is in the shape of events. Readers feel it as a small shock followed by understanding.

*Dramatic irony* is a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows. When Poe's narrator sits the police over the body and chats calmly, the reader knows what is under the floor and the officers do not. In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows Juliet is only drugged when Romeo finds her and believes she is dead. Dramatic irony makes the reader an anxious witness who wants to shout at the page.

To find irony, look for gaps: between words and meaning, between expectation and result, between the character's knowledge and yours. Then ask what the gap is for. Irony can be funny, cruel, or heartbreaking. O. Henry's gap ends in tenderness, since the failed gifts prove the love. Poe's gap ends in horror. Naming the kind of irony is the first step; explaining its effect is the interpretation.

words.d: saying one thing while meaning the opposite, with the listener expected to understand
a gap between what is expected to happen and what actually happens
a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows
verbal irony with a cutting edge, meant to mock or wound

look.title: Sorting the Gaps
look.text: 1. A fire station burns down. 2. A coach watching his team lose by forty points says, Great defense, everyone. 3. In a film, a character says she has never felt safer while the audience can see a figure behind the curtain.
look.prompt: Name the kind of irony in each case. Which one depends on the audience knowing more than the character?

check.q: In The Gift of the Magi, each gift is made useless by the other. Which kind of irony is that?
choices: Verbal irony
Dramatic irony
Sarcasm
Situational irony
check.why: The gap is between what the characters expected and what events produced, not in anyone's words.

check.q: What makes dramatic irony different from the other two kinds?
choices: It depends on the audience knowing more than a character
It only appears in plays
It is always funny
It depends on the speaker meaning the opposite of what is said
check.why: Dramatic irony is a knowledge gap between the audience and a character on the page or stage.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is the final step in reading irony?
choices: Deciding whether the author was joking
Explaining what the gap does to the reader
Counting how many times the irony appears
Replacing the ironic words with plain ones
check.why: Naming the kind is the start; interpretation means saying what the irony accomplishes.

lessons.title: Ambiguity on Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Ambiguity is a text's deliberate openness to more than one meaning, and it differs from vagueness because each meaning is supported by the words.
reading: Robert Frost's poem The Road Not Taken, published in 1916, ends with a speaker saying he took the road less traveled by, and that it has made all the difference. Millions of people have read that as a cheer for bold choices. But earlier in the same poem, the speaker admits that the two roads were worn really about the same. So did he take the harder road, or is he an old man telling himself a flattering story about a choice that was never that different? The poem supports both readings. That is *ambiguity*.

Ambiguity is not the same as confusion. A *vague* sentence has no clear meaning because the writer was careless: The thing happened somewhere and it was bad. An ambiguous line has two or more clear meanings, each supported by the words, and the writer meant the reader to hold both. The test is evidence. If you can point to lines that support reading A and other lines that support reading B, the text is ambiguous. If you cannot support either, it is vague.

Writers use ambiguity because life is ambiguous. Frost's speaker will tell the story with a sigh, ages and ages hence, and the poem does not say whether the sigh is satisfaction or regret. A reader who wants a single answer will be frustrated. A reader who can say, this poem is about how we turn our choices into stories afterward, has found the meaning that includes both readings. Often the best interpretation is the one that explains why the ambiguity is there.

When you meet an ambiguous passage, do not pick a side too fast. Write both readings down. Find the evidence for each. Then ask what the text gains from leaving the question open. That question is usually the door into the text's deepest subject.

words.d: deliberate openness to two or more meanings, each supported by the text
unclear because the writer was careless or imprecise; not the same as ambiguous
a reading of a text's meaning that is supported by evidence from the text

look.title: The Famous Ending
look.text: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference.
look.cite: Robert Frost, The Road Not Taken, 1916
look.prompt: Earlier the poem says the roads were worn about the same. Does the speaker believe what he says here, or is he shaping a story? What word choices could support each reading?

check.q: What separates an ambiguous line from a vague one?
choices: An ambiguous line is longer
A vague line is always in a poem
An ambiguous line has two or more clear meanings, each supported by the words
A vague line has more than one meaning
check.why: Ambiguity is supported openness; vagueness is the absence of clear meaning.

check.q: Which detail in The Road Not Taken complicates the reading of the ending as a cheer for bold choices?
choices: The poem has four stanzas
The speaker says the two roads were worn about the same
The poem was published in 1916
The speaker is walking in autumn
check.why: If the roads were really alike, the claim that one was less traveled is a story the speaker tells later.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is often the best interpretation of an ambiguous text?
choices: The one most readers agree with
The one the author stated in an interview
The shortest one
The one that explains why the ambiguity is there
check.why: The reading that accounts for both possibilities usually names the text's real subject.

lessons.title: Satire and Its Targets
lessons.mainIdea: Satire uses exaggeration, irony and mock seriousness to expose something the writer wants the reader to condemn.
reading: In 1729 the Irish writer Jonathan Swift published a short pamphlet calmly proposing that the poor of Ireland could ease their poverty by selling their one-year-old children as food for the rich. He included recipes and cost estimates. He was not a monster. He was furious at English landlords and policies that were, in his view, already devouring the Irish poor, and he wanted readers to feel that fury through their own disgust. The pamphlet, A Modest Proposal, is the most famous piece of *satire* in the language.

Satire is writing that attacks a target, usually a human folly, a vice or an institution, by making it look ridiculous. Its main tools are *exaggeration*, which blows a flaw up until it cannot be missed, and irony, especially the mock-serious voice that says appalling things in a reasonable tone. Swift's narrator never winks. The horror comes from the reader's realization that the calm math of the proposal matches the calm math of the real policies.

Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, published in the United States in 1885, is satire with a gentler surface. Huck, a boy raised in a slaveholding society, believes helping his friend Jim escape is a sin. When he decides to help anyway, he says he will go to hell for it. Twain's target is not Huck; it is the society that taught a good-hearted boy that kindness was wickedness. The reader is meant to see what Huck cannot.

To read satire, ask three questions. What is the target? What tools make the target look absurd? And what does the writer want instead? Swift wanted fair treatment for the poor; Twain wanted readers to see that a whole society's moral teaching could be upside down. Satire that misses its target becomes mere mockery. Satire that hits it changes how readers see the world, sometimes for centuries.

words.d: writing that attacks a folly, vice or institution by making it look ridiculous
making something larger or more extreme than it is, to expose it
a tone that treats an absurd or terrible idea with calm reasonableness, on purpose
the person, habit or institution a satire is meant to expose

look.title: A Proposal Made in Cold Blood
look.text: Swift's narrator argues, with numbers and a reasonable tone, that a healthy child of one year is a delicious and nourishing food, and that selling infants would relieve the poor of the cost of raising them while giving landlords, who have already devoured most of the parents, a claim on the children.
look.cite: Jonathan Swift, A Modest Proposal, 1729 (described, not quoted)
look.prompt: Swift never says the proposal is horrible. Why is a calm voice more effective here than an angry one?

check.q: What is the real target of Swift's A Modest Proposal?
choices: Irish parents who have too many children
Cooks who use bad recipes
Landlords and policies that were crushing the Irish poor
Readers who do not understand mathematics
check.why: The cannibal proposal is the tool; the target is the treatment of the poor.

check.q: In Huckleberry Finn, whom does Twain's satire attack when Huck says he will go to hell for helping Jim?
choices: The society that taught Huck kindness was sin
Huck, for being weak
Jim, for running away
Readers who like adventure stories
check.why: Huck's good act looks like sin only because his society's teaching is upside down.

check.q: Which tool does Swift use most heavily in A Modest Proposal?
choices: Flashback
A mock-serious tone that treats a terrible idea reasonably
Dramatic irony about what characters know
A stream of loosely connected thoughts
check.why: The narrator never winks; the calm reasonableness is what produces the reader's disgust.

lessons.title: Motif and Symbol
lessons.mainIdea: A motif is a repeated element that builds meaning across a text; a symbol is a concrete thing that stands for something larger.
reading: Here is a short model story, written for this lesson. Ana counted the locks on the apartment door: three. Her father had added the third after the break-in. At school she found the locker jammed and kicked it until the lock gave. At night she lay awake listening to the deadbolt turn as her mother came home, and only then could she sleep. In the last scene, moving out at eighteen, she leaves her key on the counter and pulls the door shut behind her without locking it.

The locks are a *motif*: an element, such as an object, phrase, image or sound, that repeats across a text and gathers meaning as it repeats. One lock is a detail. Three locks, a jammed locker and a deadbolt are a pattern, and a pattern is a message. Each time the motif returns, the reader carries the earlier appearances with it. That is why the final unlocked door means so much: it is the first time the pattern breaks.

A *symbol* is a concrete thing that stands for something beyond itself. In Ana's story, the locks come to symbolize fear and the wish for safety, and the unlocked door symbolizes trust or release. The difference between motif and symbol is roughly the difference between a pattern and a meaning: the motif is what repeats, the symbol is what the repetition comes to stand for. Often the same object is both.

Two cautions. First, a symbol must be earned by the text; a reader who declares that every bird means freedom is not interpreting, only labeling. Ask whether the text itself connects the object to the idea, through repetition, placement or a character's attention. Second, symbols are rarely equations. The locks do not mean exactly one thing. They mean fear, and care, and the father's love, and the daughter's cage, all at once. Good interpretation keeps that fullness.

words.d: an object, image, phrase or sound that repeats through a text and gathers meaning
a concrete thing in a text that stands for something larger than itself
a repetition the reader can notice and track across a text

look.title: How Often the Lock Returns
look.cite: counted for this lesson in the Ana passage
look.prompt: Lock words appear four times, yet the key appears once, at the end. Why might a single late appearance carry more weight than repeated early ones?

check.q: What is a motif?
choices: The moral of a story
An element that repeats through a text and gathers meaning
A character who changes
The place a story is set
check.why: A motif is a repeated element; its meaning builds each time it returns.

check.q: Why does the unlocked door at the end of Ana's story carry so much meaning?
choices: It is the first time the pattern of locks breaks
It is described in the longest paragraph
Doors are always symbols of death
It is the only door in the story
check.why: The reader carries every earlier lock to the final scene, so the break in the pattern is the message.

check.q: What does the lesson say a reader must do before calling an object a symbol?
choices: Look the object up in a dictionary of symbols
Check what the author said in interviews
Show that the text itself connects the object to an idea
Find the object in the title
check.why: A symbol must be earned by the text through repetition, placement or attention; otherwise the reader is only labeling.

lessons.title: Archetypes
lessons.mainIdea: An archetype is a character, situation or image that recurs across many cultures and centuries of stories, and recognizing it lets you see how a text uses or breaks the pattern.
reading: A young person leaves home, meets a guide, crosses into a dangerous world, faces a test, and returns changed. You have read this story many times, with a hobbit, a Jedi, a girl from Kansas, a boy with a lightning scar. It is older than any of them. It is in the story of Odysseus and in folk tales collected in every part of the world. A pattern this widespread is an *archetype*: a character type, plot or image that appears across cultures and centuries, as if human beings keep needing to tell it.

Common archetypal characters include the hero, the mentor, the trickster, the outcast and the tyrant. Common archetypal situations include the journey, the fall from grace, the return home and the sacrifice. Common archetypal images include light and dark, the garden, the flood, the desert. None of these belongs to any one writer. A writer draws on them the way a musician draws on a familiar chord.

Recognizing an archetype is useful only if you go one step further and ask how this text uses it. Huck Finn is a journey story, but Huck's guide is an enslaved man the society calls property, and the river carries the two of them deeper into slave territory, not toward safety. Twain takes the oldest pattern and turns it so that the reader feels the wrongness of the world the pattern moves through. The interest is never in the archetype alone. It is in the variation.

A caution: archetypes are broad, so almost any story can be forced into one. If you claim a character is a trickster, show the tricks and what they cost or reveal. If you claim a journey, show the crossing, the test and the return, or show which of those the text refuses to give. The pattern is the starting point. The evidence is still the work.

words.d: a character type, situation or image that recurs across many cultures and centuries of stories
the archetypal guide who prepares or advises the hero
an archetypal character who breaks rules and uses cleverness, often exposing others' foolishness
the specific way one text changes or twists a familiar pattern

look.title: The Journey, Turned
look.text: A journey story usually moves a hero from home into danger and back to a home that now looks different. Huck's raft floats south, away from freedom for Jim. There is no true home to return to; Huck ends by planning to run off again.
look.prompt: Which parts of the archetypal journey does Twain keep, and which does he refuse? What might each refusal be saying?

check.q: What makes a pattern an archetype rather than just a common plot?
choices: It was invented by a famous author
It only appears in fantasy novels
It is always about a war
It recurs across many cultures and centuries of storytelling
check.why: Archetypes belong to no one writer; they appear again and again across human cultures.

check.q: According to the lesson, where does the interest of an archetype lie for a reader?
choices: In naming the archetype correctly
In how a specific text uses or varies the pattern
In finding the oldest version
In proving the author knew the pattern
check.why: Recognition is only the first step; the variation is what the text means.

check.q: Which is an example of an archetypal situation, according to the lesson?
choices: The trickster
The journey
The desert
The mentor
check.why: The journey, the fall and the return are situations; the trickster and mentor are character types, and the desert is an image.

lessons.title: Allusion
lessons.mainIdea: An allusion is a brief reference to another text, person or event that borrows that reference's meaning for the new text.
reading: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, from 1851, begins with three words: Call me Ishmael. Readers in 1851 knew their Bibles, and they knew Ishmael as the son of Abraham cast out into the wilderness with his mother, an outsider who survived. Without a sentence of explanation, Melville's narrator has told you he is a wanderer, an outcast, and a survivor. That is an *allusion*: a brief reference to a person, place, event or text outside the work that brings its meaning along.

Allusions are a kind of compression. A writer who calls a character a Judas has said in one word what would otherwise take a paragraph about betrayal by a friend. Writers allude to scripture, to mythology, to Shakespeare, to history, to songs and to other novels. The reference works only if the reader catches it, which is why allusions from a century ago can sail past us today, and why annotated editions and a quick search matter.

To read an allusion, do three things. Identify the reference: who or what is being named? Recall what that reference means in its own source: Ishmael, the outcast who lived. Then ask how that meaning changes the new text: a narrator who calls himself Ishmael expects to be cast out and to endure, and Moby-Dick ends with him as the only survivor. The allusion at the first sentence has predicted the last page.

Allusions can also be ironic, when the writer sets a small thing beside a great reference to make the small thing look absurd, or a great reference beside a small thing to make it heroic. A teenager's lost phone described in the language of Paradise Lost is comic. A cleaning woman's day told with echoes of Odysseus is something else. In each case the borrowed meaning does work, and the interpretation is in saying what work.

words.d: a brief reference to a person, event, place or text outside the work that carries its meaning into the work
saying a great deal in few words
a version of a text with notes that explain references and hard words

look.title: Three Words That Predict a Book
look.prompt: The narrator does not say 'My name is Ishmael.' He says 'Call me.' What does that small difference add to the allusion?

check.q: What does the allusion in 'Call me Ishmael' tell a reader who knows the biblical story?
choices: The narrator is a sailor
The narrator is rich
The narrator is an outcast and a survivor
The narrator is lying about his name
check.why: The biblical Ishmael was cast into the wilderness and lived; the allusion brings that meaning to the narrator.

check.q: Why does the lesson call allusion a kind of compression?
choices: Allusions shorten the words in a sentence
One reference carries meaning that would otherwise take a paragraph
Allusions always appear in the first line
Allusions are printed in smaller type
check.why: Calling someone a Judas says in one word what a full explanation of betrayal would take much longer to say.

check.q: What is the third step in reading an allusion, according to the lesson?
choices: Ask how the reference's meaning changes the new text
Identify the reference
Recall what the reference means in its source
Look up the author's biography
check.why: Identify, recall, then apply: the interpretation lies in what the borrowed meaning does in the new text.

lessons.title: Stream of Consciousness
lessons.mainIdea: Stream of consciousness narration tries to put the reader inside a mind as it actually moves, with its jumps, repetitions and half-finished thoughts.
reading: Here is a passage written for this lesson. Bus late again and the cold coming through the shoe where the sole split, should have taped it, Mom said tape it, the number 9 and then the 66, Chicago Avenue, the man with the dog every morning, what does he do, does he work, test at nine, the test, I knew the causes of the war yesterday, tariffs, Fort Sumter, the shoe. No period until the end. No commas where a careful writer would put them. The thoughts run into one another the way real thoughts do.

This is *stream of consciousness*, a technique that tries to reproduce the flow of a mind: its associations, its interruptions, the way a split shoe leads to a mother's voice leads to a bus number leads to a history test. Writers in the early twentieth century, including James Joyce and Virginia Woolf, pushed the technique far, sometimes dropping punctuation for pages. The point is not to be difficult. The point is that a mind is not a tidy paragraph, and a story that pretends otherwise is leaving something out.

Reading stream of consciousness takes a different posture. Do not hunt for the topic sentence. Instead track the associations: what leads to what, and what keeps returning. In the passage above, the shoe returns three times. The test returns twice. A reader who notices that the character's mind keeps sliding from the test back to the shoe has learned something about worry that the character never states. The technique is a window into a mind, and the reader's job is to look through it and describe what they see.

You will meet this technique more fully in later study. For now, be able to recognize it: long unbroken sentences, thoughts triggering thoughts, missing connectors, shifts in time within a line. And be able to say what it does: it puts the reader inside a mind so that the reader knows the character from within, before the character has understood a thing.

words.d: narration that reproduces the flow of a character's thoughts, with jumps, repetitions and missing connectors
the way one thought leads to another by a link of memory, sound or feeling
inside a character's mind; interior monologue is thought presented as speech to oneself

look.title: A Mind on a Cold Morning
look.text: Bus late again and the cold coming through the shoe where the sole split, should have taped it, Mom said tape it, the number 9 and then the 66, Chicago Avenue, the man with the dog every morning, what does he do, does he work, test at nine, the test, I knew the causes of the war yesterday, tariffs, Fort Sumter, the shoe.
look.prompt: The passage never says the character is anxious. What details and returns let you know it anyway?

check.q: Which feature is typical of stream of consciousness narration?
choices: Short sentences with clear topic sentences
Thoughts that trigger other thoughts, with connectors left out
A narrator who describes only what can be seen from outside
Events told strictly in the order they happened
check.why: The technique follows the mind's associations rather than the rules of a tidy paragraph.

check.q: In the model passage, what does the repeated return to the shoe suggest?
choices: The character is thinking about buying new shoes
The character has forgotten the test
The character's worry keeps pulling the mind back to something small
The bus route passes a shoe store
check.why: The repeated return shows a worried mind that slides from the test to a small physical discomfort and back.

check.q: How should a reader approach a stream of consciousness passage, according to the lesson?
choices: Track what leads to what and what keeps returning
Find the topic sentence and skip the rest
Rewrite it with correct punctuation first
Read only the first and last lines
check.why: The associations and the returns are where the meaning lives.

lessons.title: Weighing Two Readings
lessons.mainIdea: When a text supports more than one interpretation, the stronger reading is the one that accounts for more of the text and forces less of it.
reading: Two students read The Tell-Tale Heart. One says the story is about guilt: the narrator's own conscience, in the form of the beating heart, forces him to confess. The other says it is about madness: there is no guilt, only a diseased mind hearing sounds that are not there. Both readings are reasonable. Both cite the text. So which is right? The honest answer is that interpretation is not a coin flip between equal guesses. Some readings are stronger than others, and there are tests.

The first test is coverage: how much of the text does the reading explain? The guilt reading explains the confession, but it must work hard to explain why the narrator feels no guilt at all before the police arrive. The madness reading explains the seven nights of staring and the hearing of a dead heart, and it also explains the confession, since the narrator cannot tell his own heartbeat from the corpse's. A reading that accounts for more, with less strain, is stronger.

The second test is *textual evidence* versus outside assumption. If a reading depends on something the text never shows, such as the old man secretly deserving it, the reading is standing on air. The third test is whether the reading can survive its best objection. State the opposing reading fairly, then show what it cannot explain. A reading that has never faced an objection has not been tested.

Notice that the two readings of Poe may not be enemies. Perhaps the story is about a mind that experiences guilt as sound, so that madness and conscience are the same thing. A synthesis that keeps the strengths of both is often the strongest interpretation of all. But it must still meet the tests: coverage, evidence, and survival under objection. The rule is not that all readings are equal. The rule is that every reading must earn its place.

words.d: specific words, lines or details from the text used to support a reading
how much of a text an interpretation can explain
the strongest reason someone might reject a reading
a reading that combines the strengths of two interpretations

look.title: Two Readings, One Story
rows: Details the guilt reading explains easily
Details the guilt reading must strain to explain
Details the madness reading explains easily
Details the madness reading must strain to explain
look.cite: counted for this lesson from six key details: the vulture eye, seven nights of watching, the calm dismemberment, the chat with police, the heartbeat, the confession
look.prompt: Coverage favors one reading here. Which single detail do you think the madness reading strains on, and could a synthesis fix it?

check.q: What does the coverage test ask about an interpretation?
choices: How many pages the interpretation takes to write
How much of the text the reading explains without strain
Whether the author would agree
How many other readers share the reading
check.why: A reading that accounts for more of the text with less forcing is stronger.

check.q: Which reading of Poe's story does the lesson say stands on air?
choices: The guilt reading
The madness reading
The synthesis reading
A reading that depends on the old man secretly deserving his death
check.why: The text never shows that; a reading resting on something the text does not contain lacks evidence.

check.q: According to the lesson, what should a reader do with the opposing reading?
choices: Ignore it so the argument stays focused
State it fairly and show what it cannot explain
Assume it is equally correct
Mention it only in the conclusion
check.why: A reading that has never faced its best objection has not been tested.

lessons.title: Writing an Interpretation
lessons.mainIdea: An interpretive essay argues how a text means, with a debatable claim, evidence from the text, and reasoning that connects the two.
reading: A weak thesis says: The Tell-Tale Heart uses an unreliable narrator. That is true and no one would argue with it, which is exactly the problem. A strong thesis says: In The Tell-Tale Heart, the narrator's insistence on his own calm is the very evidence Poe uses to convict him, so that the story makes the reader the judge the narrator fears. Now someone could disagree. Now there is something to prove. An interpretation is an *argument*, and an argument needs a claim that could be wrong.

The claim should be about how the text means, not merely what it contains. Not: the story has a symbol. Rather: the heartbeat works as a symbol of guilt the narrator cannot name, and Poe times its return so that it grows as the narrator's confidence grows. The second version connects a device to an effect. That connection, device to effect to meaning, is the spine of every interpretive paragraph.

Evidence means quotation and close description. Quote short, then explain. Do not let a quotation do your arguing; a quotation is a fact, and the reasoning is where you show what the fact proves. A useful paragraph shape: claim for this paragraph, quoted or described evidence, two or three sentences explaining how the evidence supports the claim, and a sentence linking to the thesis. Then treat the strongest objection honestly in its own paragraph and answer it.

Comparing two texts on a theme follows the same rules with one addition: the claim must be about the relationship. Not: both Poe and Frost write about the mind. Rather: Poe's narrator and Frost's speaker both rewrite their pasts, but Poe punishes the rewriting while Frost leaves it open, and that difference reveals two views of self-knowledge. Then every paragraph must keep both texts in play. An interpretation that argues is not a report on a book. It is your best case for a way of seeing it, made with the text in your hand.

words.d: the main debatable claim an essay sets out to prove
a claim supported by evidence and reasoning, open to disagreement
careful attention to the specific words and details of a passage
the sentences that explain how a piece of evidence supports a claim

look.title: Weak Claim, Strong Claim
look.text: Claim A: Frost's The Road Not Taken uses ambiguity. Claim B: Frost's The Road Not Taken uses the gap between the middle stanzas and the ending to show how memory flatters the choices we made, so the famous last lines are a story the speaker tells himself.
look.prompt: Why can no one argue with Claim A? What in Claim B could a reader dispute, and what evidence would settle it?

check.q: What is wrong with the thesis 'The Tell-Tale Heart uses an unreliable narrator'?
choices: It is false
It is too long
No one could disagree with it, so there is nothing to prove
It mentions the title
check.why: An interpretation is an argument, and an argument needs a claim that could be wrong.

check.q: What should a quotation do in an interpretive paragraph, according to the lesson?
choices: Serve as a fact that the writer's reasoning then explains
Replace the need for reasoning
Appear at the end of every paragraph
Be as long as possible to show thorough reading
check.why: A quotation is evidence; the reasoning shows what the evidence proves.

check.q: What extra requirement applies when a claim compares two texts?
choices: The claim must name the publication dates
The claim must be about the relationship between the texts
Only one text may be quoted
The claim must praise both texts
check.why: Saying both texts share a theme is a report; a comparative claim must say how they differ or connect and why that matters.

review.q: A story begins with the funeral and then goes back to tell the life. Which device is this?
choices: Chronological order
Satire
Dramatic irony
Beginning in medias res
review.why: Starting in the middle or at the end and then going back is in medias res.

review.q: Why does Poe's narrator count as unreliable?
choices: He tells the story in the past tense
His own details contradict his claim to be sane
He is a minor character
He never describes the old man
review.why: The reader builds a second, truer story out of what the narrator lets slip.

review.q: In a film, the audience sees the villain hiding as the hero says she feels perfectly safe. That is an example of
choices: verbal irony
situational irony
dramatic irony
sarcasm
review.why: The audience knows more than the character; that gap is dramatic irony.

review.q: Which statement about ambiguity is correct?
choices: Each of its meanings is supported by the text
It is another name for vagueness
It occurs only in poetry
It means the author was unsure what to say
review.why: Ambiguity is deliberate, supported openness; vagueness is careless lack of meaning.

review.q: What is the target of a satire?
choices: The reader who fails to laugh
The narrator of the satire
The characters' costumes
The folly, vice or institution the writer wants exposed
review.why: Satire attacks a target by making it look ridiculous; Swift's target was the treatment of the Irish poor.

review.q: What is the main difference between a motif and a symbol?
choices: A motif is a repeated element; a symbol is what something stands for
A motif is a person; a symbol is an object
A motif appears once; a symbol repeats
There is no difference
review.why: The motif is the pattern; the symbol is the meaning the pattern comes to carry. Often one object is both.

review.q: 'Call me Ishmael' is an example of
choices: stream of consciousness
allusion
a flashback
situational irony
review.why: The name refers to a biblical outcast and survivor, and brings that meaning into the novel.

review.q: Which interpretation of a text is strongest, according to the chapter?
choices: The one most classmates chose
The one that explains the most of the text with the least forcing and survives its best objection
The one that uses the most literary terms
The one closest to the author's biography
review.why: Coverage, textual evidence and survival under objection are the tests; readings must earn their place.
